questions.stem:
A 42-year-old man has had 1 day of abrupt fever, chills, muscle aches, headache, and cough in January. A rapid molecular test of a nasal swab is positive for influenza A. He is prescribed an oral drug twice daily for 5 days. In cell culture, the drug does not stop the virus from entering cells or copying its genome, but newly made virions remain stuck to the surface of the infected cell.

Which viral protein does this drug inhibit?
choices: Hemagglutinin, which attaches the virus to host cells
Neuraminidase, which cleaves sialic acid to release progeny virus
Polymerase acidic protein, which has endonuclease activity
Thymidine kinase, which phosphorylates nucleoside analogs
DNA terminase complex, which packages new viral genomes

explain.html:
The drug is oseltamivir, an oral neuraminidase inhibitor given twice daily for 5 days as treatment (once daily for 10 days as prophylaxis). Influenza hemagglutinin attaches the virus to host cells, and neuraminidase lets newly formed virus leave by cleaving sialic acid from glycoproteins on the cell surface.

By blocking neuraminidase, oseltamivir, zanamivir, and peramivir prevent release of virus from infected cells, so virions stay tethered and cannot spread. They act on influenza A and B, and resistance arises from mutations in neuraminidase, more often in influenza A.
why: Hemagglutinin is the attachment protein; the drug did not block entry.
The polymerase acidic endonuclease is the target of baloxavir, which blocks viral transcription and replication.
Thymidine kinase is a herpesvirus enzyme that activates acyclovir, not an influenza protein.
The DNA terminase complex is a cytomegalovirus target of letermovir.
explain.takeaway: Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir) prevent release of influenza A and B virions from infected cells.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old woman with moderate persistent asthma develops influenza B. She is started on an inhaled antiviral twice daily. Within an hour of the second dose she has chest tightness and wheezing, and her peak flow drops by 30%. Her asthma had been well controlled.

Which antiviral would be the better choice for her?
choices: Inhaled zanamivir at a lower dose
Oral acyclovir
Intravenous foscarnet
Oral valganciclovir
Oral oseltamivir

explain.html:
The inhaled neuraminidase inhibitor is zanamivir. All neuraminidase inhibitors share effects such as insomnia, vertigo, and neuropsychiatric events, but zanamivir's unique adverse effect is bronchospasm because it is delivered to the airways, which makes it a poor choice in a patient with asthma.

Oral oseltamivir has the same mechanism and covers influenza A and B without the inhaled route, so it is the better option for her. The other drugs listed target herpesviruses, not influenza.
why: Lowering the dose of zanamivir keeps the inhaled route that triggers bronchospasm.
Acyclovir treats herpes simplex and varicella zoster virus, not influenza.
Foscarnet treats cytomegalovirus and resistant herpesvirus infections, not influenza.
Valganciclovir is used for cytomegalovirus, not influenza.
explain.takeaway: Inhaled zanamivir can cause bronchospasm, so oral oseltamivir is preferred for influenza in patients with asthma.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 17-year-old boy with uncomplicated influenza A is given a single oral dose of an antiviral. The prodrug is converted to an active form that inhibits the endonuclease activity of a selective polymerase acidic protein that the virus needs for transcription. He swallows the tablet with a large glass of milk and an antacid for an upset stomach.

Which of the following is the most likely consequence of how he took the dose?
choices: Bronchospasm from airway delivery
Increased conversion to the active drug
Nephrotoxicity from crystal formation
Reduced drug absorption
Visual disturbances and hallucinations

explain.html:
The drug is baloxavir marboxil, a prodrug converted to baloxavir, which inhibits the endonuclease of the polymerase acidic protein needed for influenza A and B transcription. It is given orally as one dose because of its long half-life (about 79 hours) and is approved for uncomplicated influenza or post-exposure prophylaxis in people older than 12.

Its absorption is affected by dairy products and cations such as those in antacids, so taking it with milk and an antacid lowers the amount absorbed and can make the single dose less effective. Its main adverse effects are diarrhea and nasopharyngitis.
why: Bronchospasm is the unique adverse effect of inhaled zanamivir.
Food and cations do not increase conversion of the prodrug; they lower absorption.
Nephrotoxicity is a concern with intravenous acyclovir, cidofovir, and foscarnet, not baloxavir.
Visual hallucinations are a unique adverse effect of voriconazole.
explain.takeaway: Baloxavir is a single-dose oral endonuclease inhibitor for influenza whose absorption is reduced by dairy products and cations.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 67-year-old man is admitted with herpes zoster involving multiple dermatomes and is started on high-dose intravenous acyclovir. On day 3 his serum creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 2.3 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3), and he is newly confused. Once he improves, the team plans to switch him to an oral drug for the rest of the course.

Which oral drug is preferred for the switch, and why?
choices: Oral acyclovir, because it has the highest bioavailability
Valacyclovir, a prodrug giving higher levels
Valganciclovir, because it avoids bone marrow suppression
Oseltamivir, because it does not need renal adjustment
Letermovir, because it does not affect the kidneys at all

explain.html:
Acyclovir and valacyclovir can cause neurotoxicity, gastrointestinal upset, myelosuppression, rash, and, with intravenous acyclovir, nephrotoxicity, which explains this patient's rising creatinine and confusion during high-dose therapy.

Oral acyclovir has poor bioavailability (15 to 30%) and must be dosed many times a day. Valacyclovir is a prodrug hydrolyzed to acyclovir by first-pass and hepatic metabolism, with oral bioavailability of about 55%. It gives higher serum levels, which also lowers the risk of resistance, and it is more convenient, so it is the usual oral choice for herpes simplex and varicella zoster.
why: Oral acyclovir has low bioavailability (15 to 30%), which is why it must be dosed several times a day.
Valganciclovir is for cytomegalovirus and causes, rather than avoids, myelosuppression.
Oseltamivir treats influenza and has no activity against varicella zoster virus.
Letermovir is used only for cytomegalovirus prophylaxis.
explain.takeaway: Intravenous acyclovir can cause nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity; valacyclovir is the preferred oral prodrug because of better bioavailability and dosing.
explain.topic: Acyclovir and valacyclovir: adverse effects and dosing
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 3 months ago has fever, diarrhea, and rising cytomegalovirus viral load in blood. He is started on an intravenous drug that must be phosphorylated first by a viral kinase encoded by UL97 and then by cellular kinases, after which it is incorporated into viral DNA and terminates chain elongation. Two weeks later his labs are checked.

Which laboratory change is most likely to be found?
choices: Rising absolute neutrophil count
Serum calcium well above the normal range
Very high serum potassium from cell lysis
Isolated rise in hemoglobin
Falling absolute neutrophil and platelet counts

explain.html:
The drug is ganciclovir, the drug of choice (with its oral prodrug valganciclovir) for cytomegalovirus (CMV) treatment and prophylaxis. It is triphosphorylated first by the CMV UL97 kinase and then by cellular kinases, and it is incorporated during viral DNA synthesis, causing chain termination. Oral ganciclovir is almost not absorbed (about 5%), so it is given intravenously, while valganciclovir is given orally.

The main adverse effect of ganciclovir and valganciclovir is myelosuppression, affecting neutrophils and platelets, with anemia also possible. Other effects include fever, nephrotoxicity, and gastrointestinal symptoms, and combining it with zidovudine or flucytosine adds to marrow toxicity.
why: Ganciclovir suppresses the marrow, so neutrophils fall rather than rise.
Ganciclovir does not raise calcium; foscarnet causes low calcium.
Ganciclovir does not cause high potassium.
Ganciclovir lowers marrow output and can cause anemia rather than raise hemoglobin.
explain.takeaway: Ganciclovir and valganciclovir (activated by CMV UL97 kinase) treat CMV, and their main adverse effect is myelosuppression.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 39-year-old man with ganciclovir-resistant cytomegalovirus retinitis is started on intravenous foscarnet. On day 5 he reports tingling around his mouth and in his fingertips, and tapping over the facial nerve causes twitching of the corner of his mouth. Creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 1.6 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3).

Which laboratory finding best explains his new symptoms?
choices: High serum calcium
Low serum sodium
High serum glucose
Low serum ionized calcium
High serum phosphate

explain.html:
Foscarnet inhibits the pyrophosphate binding site of viral DNA polymerase without needing thymidine kinase or UL97, which is why it is used for resistant herpesvirus and CMV infections. Its main adverse effects are nephrotoxicity, myelosuppression (especially anemia), and electrolyte losses: low calcium, potassium, phosphate, and magnesium.

Perioral and fingertip tingling with facial twitching are signs of low calcium. Patients on foscarnet need extra hydration and electrolyte correction, and the dose must be adjusted for kidney function.
why: Foscarnet lowers, rather than raises, serum calcium.
Low sodium is not one of foscarnet's characteristic electrolyte effects.
Foscarnet does not characteristically raise glucose; hyperglycemia was listed for peramivir.
Foscarnet lowers phosphate rather than raising it.
explain.takeaway: Foscarnet causes nephrotoxicity and losses of calcium, potassium, phosphate, and magnesium; perioral tingling signals hypocalcemia.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 50-year-old man with cytomegalovirus disease resistant to ganciclovir is to start an intravenous nucleotide analog that is converted by cellular enzymes to a diphosphate and incorporated into viral DNA. The drug has a short serum half-life but persists inside cells for a long time. The order set includes more than 1 L of intravenous saline before and during each infusion and an oral drug given with each dose.

The oral drug and the saline are given mainly to reduce which adverse effect?
choices: Bone marrow suppression
Nephrotoxicity
Visual hallucinations
Bronchospasm
Prolonged QT interval

explain.html:
The antiviral is cidofovir, a nucleotide analog converted to cidofovir diphosphate that incorporates into viral DNA and reduces DNA synthesis. Its major adverse effects are nephrotoxicity and myelosuppression, with ocular hypotony and uveitis when given into the eye.

Probenecid reduces renal excretion of cidofovir, which raises drug levels and lowers its nephrotoxicity, and generous hydration of more than 1 L before and during the infusion protects the kidneys further.
why: Cidofovir can suppress the marrow, but probenecid and saline are given to protect the kidneys.
Visual hallucinations are a unique adverse effect of voriconazole.
Bronchospasm is the unique adverse effect of inhaled zanamivir.
QT prolongation is an azole adverse effect, not the reason for probenecid and saline with cidofovir.
explain.takeaway: Cidofovir is nephrotoxic, so it is given with probenecid (reduces renal excretion and nephrotoxicity) and saline hydration.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old cytomegalovirus-seropositive man is about to undergo an allogeneic stem cell transplant. The team plans to prevent CMV reactivation with a drug that does not inhibit viral DNA polymerase. Instead it targets the viral DNA terminase complex (UL51, UL56, UL89), so new viral DNA is not processed and packaged into virions. Marrow toxicity is a major concern because his graft must engraft.

Which of the following is true of this drug?
choices: It is used for prophylaxis and has many drug interactions
It is mainly used to treat recurrent herpes simplex genital ulcers
It needs phosphorylation by the UL97 kinase to act
It is given by inhalation and can cause bronchospasm
It is used with amphotericin for cryptococcal meningitis

explain.html:
The drug is letermovir, which inhibits CMV replication by targeting the DNA terminase complex. Without terminase, viral DNA is not processed into genome-length units and packaged, and virion maturation fails. Because it does not act on DNA polymerase, it avoids the myelosuppression of ganciclovir, which matters while a stem cell graft engrafts.

Letermovir is approved for CMV prophylaxis. Its adverse effects are gastrointestinal upset, peripheral edema, fatigue, cough, and headache, and it has many drug interactions, including with immunosuppressants, amiodarone, warfarin, phenytoin, voriconazole, statins, and rifampin.
why: Herpes simplex ulcers are treated with acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir, not letermovir.
Needing UL97 phosphorylation describes ganciclovir; letermovir works without it.
Inhaled delivery and bronchospasm describe zanamivir.
Flucytosine, not letermovir, is combined with amphotericin for cryptococcal meningitis.
explain.takeaway: Letermovir blocks the CMV DNA terminase complex, is approved for prophylaxis, avoids marrow toxicity, and has many drug interactions.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 63-year-old man with leukemia and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis starts an intravenous azole that has nonlinear pharmacokinetics and requires level monitoring. On the second day he reports that colors look abnormally bright and that he saw people standing in his room who were not there. He is oriented and his electrolytes are normal.

Which drug is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
choices: Fluconazole
Isavuconazole
Voriconazole
Micafungin
Flucytosine

explain.html:
Among the azoles, voriconazole is active against Candida and Aspergillus, has nonlinear pharmacokinetics, and is monitored by drug levels. Its unique adverse effect is visual disturbance, including visual hallucinations, in addition to the azole class effects of elevated liver enzymes, hepatitis, gastrointestinal upset, and QT prolongation.

Isavuconazole is also used for Aspergillus, but its unique effect is QT shortening rather than prolongation. Fluconazole does not cover Aspergillus, and micafungin is an echinocandin used only as salvage therapy for Aspergillus.
why: Fluconazole covers Candida but not Aspergillus and is not known for visual hallucinations.
Isavuconazole covers Aspergillus, but its unique adverse effect is QT shortening.
Micafungin is an echinocandin whose adverse effects are raised liver enzymes and infusion reactions.
Flucytosine is not an azole, does not treat Aspergillus, and mainly causes marrow suppression.
explain.takeaway: Voriconazole treats aspergillosis, needs level monitoring because of nonlinear kinetics, and uniquely causes visual disturbances and hallucinations.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 66-year-old man with a long-term urinary catheter has fever, flank pain, and pyuria, and urine culture grows a Candida species. He is started on intravenous micafungin. After 5 days his urine culture remains positive and his symptoms have not improved, even though the isolate is reported as sensitive to micafungin in the laboratory.

Which property of the drug best explains the treatment failure?
choices: Rapid renal clearance before it reaches the bladder wall
Bacterial contamination of the urine sample
Inactivation of the drug by stomach acid
Resistance caused by thymidine kinase loss
Poor penetration into the urinary tract

explain.html:
Micafungin is an echinocandin. Echinocandins are given only intravenously and distribute widely to tissues, but they have no penetration into the central nervous system or the urine, and they are eliminated mostly by hepatic metabolism rather than by the kidney.

That is why a drug active against the isolate in the laboratory fails to clear a urinary Candida infection. An echinocandin is a poor choice for fungal infection of the urinary tract or the central nervous system.
why: Echinocandins are cleared mostly by the liver, not by the kidney, so little reaches the urine.
The culture grows Candida, and the problem is drug delivery, not contamination.
Micafungin is given intravenously, so stomach acid does not affect it.
Thymidine kinase loss causes acyclovir resistance in herpes simplex, not echinocandin failure.
explain.takeaway: Echinocandins do not penetrate the urine or central nervous system and are cleared by the liver, so they are not used for urinary or CNS fungal infections.
explain.topic: Echinocandins: no CNS or urinary penetration
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old man with advanced immunosuppression is treated for invasive mold infection with an intravenous antifungal that binds a sterol in the fungal cell membrane. After 10 days his labs are checked.

Test: Result: Reference range
Creatinine: 2.1 mg/dL: 0.7 to 1.3 mg/dL
Potassium: 2.8 mEq/L: 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L
Magnesium: 1.2 mg/dL: 1.7 to 2.2 mg/dL
Bicarbonate: 16 mEq/L: 22 to 28 mEq/L
Hemoglobin: 9.8 g/dL: 13.5 to 17.5 g/dL

Which change in therapy would most likely reduce this toxicity while keeping the same drug?
choices: Switching to a liposomal formulation and giving saline
Adding probenecid before each infusion to slow renal excretion
Giving the drug orally instead of intravenously
Adding flucytosine to lower the dose
Pre-medicating with diphenhydramine

explain.html:
An antifungal that binds ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane is amphotericin B, a polyene. Its nephrotoxic effects are dose limiting: it decreases the glomerular filtration rate and causes renal tubular acidosis with potassium and magnesium wasting, and anemia can result from reduced renal production of erythropoietin. This patient shows every one of those findings.

Saline infusion may reduce renal damage, and liposomal formulations of amphotericin B have reduced nephrotoxic effects. Pre-medication with diphenhydramine, acetaminophen or an NSAID, and hydrocortisone, with a slower infusion, addresses infusion reactions (fever, chills, rigors), not kidney injury.
why: Probenecid is given with cidofovir to reduce its nephrotoxicity, not with amphotericin.
Amphotericin B is given only intravenously.
Flucytosine is paired with amphotericin for cryptococcal meningitis, not as a kidney-sparing strategy, and it adds marrow toxicity.
Diphenhydramine pre-medication prevents infusion reactions such as chills and rigors, not kidney injury.
explain.takeaway: Amphotericin B causes dose-limiting nephrotoxicity (low GFR, RTA, potassium and magnesium wasting, anemia), reduced by liposomal formulations and saline loading.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 38-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy has painful, enlarging genital ulcers. Viral PCR of a swab is positive for herpes simplex virus 2. Despite 10 days of high-dose valacyclovir the lesions keep growing. Testing of the isolate shows a mutant virus that lacks the enzyme that normally performs the first phosphorylation of the drug.

Which drug is most appropriate now?
choices: Famciclovir
Ganciclovir
Foscarnet
Penciclovir cream
Oseltamivir

explain.html:
Acyclovir, and valacyclovir, its prodrug, are guanosine analogs that are first phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase (TK), then by human enzymes, to acyclovir triphosphate, which competes for viral DNA polymerase and terminates viral DNA synthesis. Resistance comes from viral mutants deficient in TK or with reduced affinity of the polymerase for acyclovir triphosphate.

A TK-deficient virus cannot activate acyclovir or other drugs that depend on viral TK, such as famciclovir and penciclovir. Foscarnet inhibits the pyrophosphate binding site of viral DNA polymerase directly and does not require TK for activation, so it remains active.
why: Famciclovir is converted to penciclovir, which also needs viral thymidine kinase, so the mutant resists it.
Ganciclovir also depends on viral kinase phosphorylation and is the drug of choice for cytomegalovirus, not thymidine kinase-deficient herpes simplex.
Penciclovir needs viral thymidine kinase, and the cream is only for oral lesions.
Oseltamivir inhibits influenza neuraminidase and has no activity against herpes simplex.
explain.takeaway: Acyclovir needs viral thymidine kinase for activation; TK-deficient herpes simplex is treated with foscarnet, which does not need TK.
explain.topic: Acyclovir resistance: thymidine kinase and foscarnet
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old woman 4 months after a stem cell transplant has cytomegalovirus viremia that keeps rising despite 3 weeks of intravenous ganciclovir at the correct dose. Genotyping shows a mutation in the viral gene that encodes the kinase performing the first phosphorylation of ganciclovir; the viral DNA polymerase gene is normal.

Which of the following drugs would still be active against this virus?
choices: Valganciclovir
Valacyclovir
Foscarnet
Famciclovir
Oseltamivir

explain.html:
Ganciclovir must first be phosphorylated by the CMV kinase encoded by UL97. Resistance comes from mutations in UL97, or in UL54, which encodes the viral DNA polymerase. Valganciclovir is a prodrug of ganciclovir and shares the same resistance mechanisms, so a UL97 mutant resists both.

Drugs that do not need UL97 remain active. Foscarnet inhibits the pyrophosphate binding site of viral DNA polymerase directly, and cidofovir is a nucleotide analog that needs only cellular enzymes to reach its active diphosphate form. With a normal polymerase gene, both should still work.
why: Valganciclovir is converted to ganciclovir and shares its UL97 resistance.
Valacyclovir is an acyclovir prodrug for herpes simplex and varicella zoster, and it also depends on viral kinase activation.
Famciclovir is converted to penciclovir, which depends on viral kinase activation and is not a CMV drug.
Oseltamivir targets influenza neuraminidase, not CMV.
explain.takeaway: CMV resistant to ganciclovir through a UL97 mutation remains sensitive to foscarnet and cidofovir, which do not need UL97 for activation.
explain.topic: CMV with UL97 mutation: drugs that bypass the viral kinase
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 46-year-old woman who received a liver transplant takes tacrolimus, and her levels have been stable. She develops invasive aspergillosis and starts a drug that inhibits the fungal enzyme that removes a methyl group at position 14 of lanosterol. One week later she has a tremor, and her creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 1.9 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1). Her tacrolimus trough level is far above target.

Which of the following best explains the rise in tacrolimus level?
choices: The antifungal binds ergosterol and damages the renal tubules
The antifungal inhibits the enzyme that metabolizes tacrolimus
The antifungal displaces tacrolimus from albumin binding sites in blood
The antifungal induces the enzyme that clears tacrolimus
Aspergillus infection directly blocks tacrolimus excretion

explain.html:
Inhibiting 14-alpha demethylation of lanosterol blocks ergosterol synthesis and disrupts the fungal cell membrane: this is the mechanism of the azoles. For aspergillosis the azole is voriconazole (also posaconazole or isavuconazole).

Azoles are inhibitors of cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4), so they raise levels of drugs that are CYP3A4 substrates, such as immunosuppressants, warfarin, phenytoin, and direct oral anticoagulants. Here, the azole slowed tacrolimus metabolism, and the high tacrolimus level caused tremor and kidney injury. Azole starts in transplant patients require a check for drug interactions.
why: Binding ergosterol is the mechanism of amphotericin B, a polyene, not of the azoles, and it does not change tacrolimus levels.
Protein-binding displacement is not the mechanism of this azole interaction.
Azoles inhibit, rather than induce, CYP3A4; induction would lower tacrolimus levels.
The infection itself does not block tacrolimus excretion; the drug interaction explains the change.
explain.takeaway: Azoles inhibit lanosterol 14-alpha demethylase and also inhibit CYP3A4, raising levels of substrates such as tacrolimus and warfarin.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 71-year-old woman in the intensive care unit with a central venous catheter develops fever and hypotension. Blood cultures grow a yeast. She was started on fluconazole, but she remains febrile and cultures stay positive. The laboratory identifies the isolate as Candida glabrata. She has no signs of meningitis or urinary infection.

Which drug class is the best choice now, and how does it act?
choices: Echinocandin; inhibits beta-1,3-glucan synthase in the cell wall
Polyene; inhibits 14-alpha demethylation of lanosterol
Neuraminidase inhibitor; prevents release from infected cells
Antimetabolite; used alone as monotherapy for yeasts
Higher-dose fluconazole; binds ergosterol to form membrane pores

explain.html:
Fluconazole covers most Candida species, but Candida glabrata (and Candida auris) are spectrum exceptions, which explains the persistent candidemia. Echinocandins (micafungin, caspofungin, anidulafungin, rezafungin) are active against Candida including glabrata and are used for invasive candidiasis.

Echinocandins inhibit the synthesis of beta-1,3-glucan, a critical component of the fungal cell wall. They are given intravenously, distribute widely, and are cleared by the liver, with raised liver enzymes and infusion reactions as adverse effects.
why: Polyenes bind ergosterol; inhibiting lanosterol demethylation is the azole mechanism.
Neuraminidase inhibitors are influenza antivirals and have no antifungal activity.
Flucytosine is an antimetabolite that is avoided as monotherapy for any fungus.
Fluconazole fails against Candida glabrata, and binding ergosterol describes amphotericin B, not azoles.
explain.takeaway: Fluconazole does not reliably cover Candida glabrata or auris; echinocandins, which inhibit beta-1,3-glucan synthesis, treat invasive candidiasis caused by them.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 31-year-old man with untreated advanced immunodeficiency has 2 weeks of headache, fever, and confusion. Opening pressure on lumbar puncture is high, and an India ink preparation of spinal fluid shows encapsulated budding yeasts. He is started on amphotericin B together with a second drug that is converted inside fungal cells to an antimetabolite. On day 10 his white cell count is 1,900/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000) and platelets 60,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000).

Which statement about the second drug is correct?
choices: It is an echinocandin that reaches the spinal fluid well
It inhibits lanosterol demethylation and causes visual hallucinations
It inhibits the viral DNA terminase complex
It is avoided as monotherapy and can suppress the bone marrow
It binds ergosterol and causes potassium wasting

explain.html:
Encapsulated budding yeast in the spinal fluid of an immunocompromised patient is cryptococcal meningitis, which is treated with amphotericin B combined with flucytosine (5-FC). Flucytosine is an antimetabolite active against Candida and Cryptococcus. It is the one antifungal that does not target the fungal membrane or cell wall.

Flucytosine is typically avoided as monotherapy for any fungus. Its adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, hepatotoxicity, aplastic anemia, and photosensitivity, and its marrow toxicity is worse when combined with zidovudine or ganciclovir.
why: Echinocandins do not penetrate the central nervous system, and the second drug here is an antimetabolite.
Lanosterol demethylase inhibition with visual hallucinations describes voriconazole.
Terminase inhibition is the mechanism of the CMV drug letermovir.
Binding ergosterol with potassium wasting describes amphotericin B, the first drug, not the second.
explain.takeaway: Cryptococcal meningitis is treated with amphotericin B plus flucytosine, an antimetabolite avoided as monotherapy that causes marrow suppression.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
